questions.stem: In the ED you are examining Fred, 64, who has suspected giant cell arteritis and a blurred right eye (acuity 6/18). You do the swinging light test in a dim room, moving the torch from one eye to the other every 2 to 3 seconds. Which finding confirms a right relative afferent pupillary defect?
options: Both pupils constrict to a near target but react poorly to the torch light
The right pupil stays dilated while the left constricts to light in either eye
Both pupils dilate as the torch swings from the left eye across to the right eye
Both pupils dilate as the torch swings from the right eye across to the left eye
questions.why: With a right optic nerve lesion, less afferent signal comes from the right eye, so both pupils dilate (paradoxically) when the light moves onto it. An RAPD shows the optic nerve or a large area of retina is affected, which is what you expect in arteritic AION.
notes: Light-near dissociation (e.g. Argyll Robertson or tectal lesions) is not an RAPD and does not localise to one optic nerve.
A pupil that stays dilated whatever eye is lit is an efferent defect (third nerve or pharmacological), not an afferent one.
Dilation when the light swings onto the left eye would mean a left RAPD, which would point to the left optic nerve, not Fred's affected right eye.

questions.stem: Fred, 64, in the ED has a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication. His right acuity has fallen from 6/18 to 6/36 over an hour. ESR 86, CRP 78. The earliest temporal artery biopsy is later this week. What is the most appropriate treatment now?
options: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily with an early rheumatology clinic review
Withhold corticosteroids until the temporal artery biopsy has been done
IV methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days, first dose now
Oral prednisolone 60 mg daily, starting after ophthalmology review tomorrow
questions.why: Suspected GCA with visual loss is a sight-threatening emergency. Give pulse IV methylprednisolone (500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days) straight away, then oral prednisolone. Never wait for the biopsy, which stays diagnostic for 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start.
notes: 15 mg is the starting dose for polymyalgia rheumatica alone. It is far too low to protect the optic nerves in GCA.
Delaying steroids risks permanent loss of the right eye and involvement of the left. The biopsy stays positive for 1 to 2 weeks after treatment starts.
Waiting until tomorrow leaves progressing ischaemic visual loss untreated, and visual involvement calls for IV pulse therapy now.

questions.stem: Fred, 64, has giant cell arteritis. His right eye has reduced acuity, an RAPD, an inferior altitudinal field defect and a pale, chalky, swollen optic disc. The left eye is normal. What is the mechanism of his right visual loss?
options: Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery, causing inner retinal infarction
Raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath to the disc
Inflammatory demyelination of the retrobulbar segment of the right optic nerve
Granulomatous occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries, infarcting the disc
questions.why: In GCA, granulomatous inflammation narrows and occludes the short posterior ciliary arteries, which supply the optic nerve head. The result is arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, with a pale, swollen disc that is infarcted and oedematous.
notes: Central retinal artery occlusion gives a pale retina with a cherry-red spot. The disc is not swollen, and the cause in GCA is arteritic rather than embolic.
Raised intracranial pressure gives bilateral papilloedema with preserved acuity early on. It does not cause a single swollen disc with an RAPD.
Optic neuritis affects younger patients, causes pain on eye movement, and the disc is usually normal (retrobulbar) or hyperaemic rather than chalky white.

questions.stem: You examine Fred's head for signs of giant cell arteritis. You are looking for a tender, thickened, pulseless right superficial temporal artery, the vessel usually sampled at biopsy. Where do you palpate it, and what is its parent artery?
options: At the anterior border of masseter over the mandible; a branch of the facial artery
Just anterior to the tragus over the zygomatic arch; external carotid terminal branch
Behind the auricle over the mastoid process; a branch of the posterior auricular artery
Above the medial eyebrow at the supraorbital notch; a branch of the ophthalmic artery
questions.why: The superficial temporal artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid. Feel it just in front of the tragus over the root of the zygomatic arch, then follow it up over the temple. In GCA it may be tender, thickened, nodular or pulseless.
notes: This is where you feel the facial artery pulse. The facial artery is a separate branch of the external carotid and is not the vessel examined or biopsied in GCA.
The posterior auricular artery runs behind the ear. It is not the temporal artery you palpate or biopsy.
The supraorbital artery comes from the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid). It is not the superficial temporal artery.
